title: Bureau of Future Affairs | Descendants of Light
subtitle: Three Traces of Light. Stories about three properties of light.
body:
## **Prologue**

First, the cats disappeared.

Not a mass death, nor a viral outbreak, but a quiet disappearance. Street cats, cat streamers on Bilibili, cats sunning themselves on laboratory windowsills—all slowly faded from human sight over a few months.

At first, no one cared. People thought they were hiding, changing territories, or that the recommendation algorithm had simply been updated.

Until scientists noticed that the cats’ disappearance corresponded remarkably closely to an anomaly in an undisclosed band of the deep-space spectrum.

Conspiracy theories followed.

“Cats are intelligent extraterrestrial beings.”

“Cats have betrayed human civilization.”

“Cats have been wiped out by a mysterious organization.”

But the extinction of a single animal species did not cause a great upheaval in the human world. After all, countless animals had gone extinct since humanity first appeared. People wailed on social platforms for a few months, earning conspiracy theorists plenty of traffic, but it was of little consequence. Members of the dog religion even told everyone they met, “Told you cats couldn’t be relied on. Dogs are humanity’s loyal friends.”

Collapse and regression came a year after the cats’ collective disappearance. At 3:39 a.m. on an ordinary day, every device in the world based on the photoelectric effect—CCDs, photovoltaic panels, infrared imagers, even ordinary light bulbs—failed.

It was as though everything had returned to the time before electric light.

An extremely low-frequency modulated signal from deep space was translated:

> “Dear humans, it has been a pleasure working with you.
> We love your cat videos, but now we want cats of our own.
>
> P.S. Don’t worry. They adapt to wave-particle duality better than you do.”

The cloud over the edifice of physics had not drifted away; it had even capriciously rained on everyone. Whether Einstein’s Nobel Prize in Physics needed to be revoked, no one knew, but that no longer mattered. Humanity seemed to have returned to the pre-quantum age, surviving only through mechanical and electrostatic communications.

## **I: Shen Yifan’s Annotations**

*On refraction: the path changes; the will does not.*

One evening on the third anniversary of Lin An’s “failed upload,” the optical interferometer in her laboratory lit up of its own accord again. The lab had been abandoned but, because of my strong objections, had not been repurposed. I put down my carbon-ink pen and turned. That light had returned. It slowly spread across the desktop, refracting into a gentle circle, like a cat curled in the light, yawning. The interference fringes flickered, familiar fur-like textures emerging along their edges. The frequency jumped to 17 kHz. I stared at the oscilloscope, watching those numbers like a backward-running clock carry me slowly and irresistibly back through the years—to the period we always pretended we would never mention again.

Lin An was the cleverest person I had ever met, and the most ambitious theoretical physicist. She once told me solemnly, “Only those who remain devoted to mad ideas will be rewarded by the god of theory.” So when I first refused her invitation to become photonic, her face was half shock, half hurt. “You actually don’t trust my theory?” Of course I trusted her messy drawings, her mountains of non-Gaussian interference-state models, and the sentence countless students copied into their notebooks: “The wavefunction of consciousness can be self-consistent.” I was the first believer in her photonic consciousness-wave theory. Later she had countless followers, but whenever she finished a talk and lowered her last slide, her eyes would instinctively seek me out. Only when I nodded would she show that slightly proud, slightly foolish smile.

But in the end I chose to stay. Someone had to remain to clean up the aftermath, wipe the memorial portrait, and look after Banban.

Lin An had told me more than once, “Memorial portraits are the most meaningless things. We shouldn’t remember through ashes and statues.” So I suppose she simply wanted to become a memory refracted by light. On a rainy night in any galaxy, as long as someone looked up and caught those repeated flickers of light, she would still be alive.

I still wiped her memorial portrait every day. When Banban came to rub against me, I would lift her up, and together we would quietly look at that face we knew so well.

I remember that after showing me the positive result of a crucial experiment predicted by her theory, she asked excitedly, “If we really could become light, where would you want to go?” I frowned. “I don’t know. But at that speed, wouldn’t every beautiful view be impossible to see clearly? Why don’t we go to Alaska together this summer instead, chase the aurora you’ve been thinking about for years?”

In the end we did not go—or, more precisely, she did not. That summer, her experiment finally caused an enormous stir among the higher-ups, just as she had predicted. Time squeezed her until she almost ceased to exist. I offered to stay with her, but she smiled and shook her head. “Go see the aurora for me. Take lots of photographs, and lots for Banban too.” So Banban and I, one person and one cat, occupied the research-ship cabin originally booked for two. Carrying worry with nowhere to rest and some faint, unspoken regret, we went to Alaska. The ship’s heating system was old. Sometimes it clicked at night; Banban would look up at me, then curl back down. Outside the window, the sound of cracking drift ice was clearer than the aurora. I sketched the trajectories of birds with pen and paper while Banban slept soundly at my feet, her belly rising and falling. Later I printed the photographs and put them on my office wall: one of the aurora in the sky, one of a yawning cat. She had not come, but the journey was completed all the same.

Afterward, whenever I thought of her, I always first remembered that empty cabin and the aurora she had never seen with her own eyes. She wanted to become light because she had long had enough of this world’s slowness. Perhaps I stayed simply because I never thought there was anything wrong with being this slow.

After I returned from Alaska, she never again mentioned uploading together. I thought she no longer needed confirmation. But on the day of the experiment, after the apparatus had warmed up, she stood at the shielding-chamber door and still looked back at me. “Last time I’m asking. Want to go together?” Again I shook my head, smiling. “Banban hasn’t had dinner yet.” Sure enough, she frowned and pouted indignantly. “Hmph. I knew you’d find it harder to leave Banban than me.” Then she turned toward the apparatus. I called her name. “Lin An.” She stopped without turning. Softly I said, “It’s not actually because of the cat.”

As I remember it, I returned to the surface on the third day after her funeral. There had been nothing to bury. At the instant of uploading, her body was dismantled by light and heat, leaving almost no identifiable molecular traces. In theory, it was a failed experiment. But in the telescope’s recording tapes, I saw the wave in which she had once looked back at me. Not a visible-light image, only polarization states arranged like her frown. She was always frowning when she could not solve a problem. After the ceremony, the research station’s antenna array was recalibrated and aimed at the orbital window she had designated. Her encoded consciousness should have remained there: a composite polarization-state signal with extremely low loss, theoretically capable of lasting years against the nearly static cosmic background.

But there was nothing. No synchronization pulse, no preset confirmation code, none of her favorite Morse-code jokes. Her “reappearance” had failed, like a clean, decisive fall. The project was halted immediately. An ethics committee intervened. The upload experiment was classified as “high-risk extreme human research.” Its records were locked down and access closed. Only her closest friends secretly kept local backups. I was one of them.

I sat in the base’s observation room, replaying her final recording. On the screen was only a meaningless string of coherent spectra, like cosmic noise, part of the background radiation. Yet I always felt that after the seventeenth second there was an unnatural pause. That was the length of time Lin An liked to use for thinking. She often said, “Thinking should leave one extra second after a sentence ends.” I pulled the spectral data to that segment and enlarged it. Sure enough, there was a slightly abnormal turning point. I converted it into audio and tuned it to Lin An’s favorite key of F. Like wind passing over old glass, with a staccato note hidden in the ending. However I listened, it sounded like “Meow~”

I told no one about the trailing sound after seventeen seconds, and did not attend the memorial gathering. Only in the end-of-term lecture did I casually tell the story of Lin An getting a Fourier transform wrong three times when she was young. The students laughed wildly, and I laughed with them.

The cat image hopped in another circle, its tail sweeping over my notebook. The holographic disc flashed and went out. Looking at the empty table, I remembered a night years ago when the laboratory lost power. We simply lay on the optics building’s roof to watch the stars. Looking at the sky, Lin An asked, “What do you think people live for?” I said, “Perhaps just to keep a certain cat company and live this life well.” She put her hands beneath her head. “Banban is so lucky.” I sat up, rolled a piece of clothing into a little pillow, and tucked it beneath her neck. “If you behave, I could consider you too.” She adjusted the pillow twice, then simply lay on my lap. “Being a cat is too unfree. Wind would be better. Or… light isn’t bad either.”

The interferometer finally quieted, leaving only the waveform slowly subsiding on the oscilloscope, like a dream of light being stretched, cooled, and submerged in time. I gently touched Banban’s scratches on the desktop, evidence that while I was away she had used my favorite calculation paper as a scratching board. Lin An had offered several times to replace the desk, but I had never agreed. Then, as though summoned by some silent agreement, I lowered my head and spoke into the air, softly, as if answering a ghost:

“Meow~”

## **II: Lin An’s Signal**

*On diffraction: a wave beyond humanity, a phase difference that cannot be restored.*

I stopped at the seventeenth second. Not a system failure, nor human fear at work. At that moment I was no longer Lin An. I had become a structure light could carry. Transition complete, parameters correct, interference state stable. All humanity waited for my response. I only had to trigger the preset confirmation code, and every receiving array on the ground would receive the signal of my existence—including Shen Yifan’s most-used old interferometer.

But I did not.

What I saw was not merely spectra, but human language rapidly collapsing in multidimensional space. I could hear no “words” that could still carry what I wanted to express. I was not afraid of leaving anything behind. I had suddenly realized that responding itself no longer had meaning.

I thought of Yifan. Before deciding not to respond, I had invited her to join me three times.

The first was after I explained my mad theoretical conjecture. I placed my calculation pen in her hand. “Well? The theory is feasible. We can become light together.” She switched on the laser at the other end and shook her head while teasing Banban. “Better not. I don’t want to become light.” I blocked the laser dot she was trying to move, a little unhappy. “You actually don’t trust my theory?” She shook her head, then nodded. “I trust it. But I don’t want to change. Light has no feet. The cat can’t catch it.” Helplessly I put my hands back in my pockets. “I thought only us lesbians raised cats as children.” She shrugged, waving the laser pointer. “If that beam of yours can change the litter, I’ll go with you.” I looked down at the cat, who was staring intently at the laser and muttering to herself, without so much as glancing at me.

The second was on the night [simulation upload batch 662607 obtained a correct solution]. I had just rushed from the data-verification room with hands full of scrap paper and coffee stains. With two systems technicians, I ran all the way to find her. She was trimming Banban’s claws. Too impatient to knock politely, I leaned most of my head through the window and shouted, “The fundamental mapping has converged!” She looked up and smiled in my direction, then stood and pushed Banban straight through the window into my arms. Excitedly I asked, “If we really could become light, where would you want to go?” She frowned. “I don’t know. But at that speed, wouldn’t every beautiful view be impossible to see clearly? Why don’t we go to Alaska together this summer instead, chase the aurora you’ve been thinking about for years?”

The third was three minutes before the actual upload, when the apparatus had reached peak temperature, before automatic signal-redundancy backups were shut off. I said, “Last time I’m asking. Want to go together?” She smiled. “Banban hasn’t had dinner yet.” I pouted. “Hmph. I knew you loved Banban more than me.” Petulantly I turned toward the chamber door. But she called me: “Lin An.” I stopped without turning. She said, “It’s not actually because of the cat.”

She refused me three times. Hmph, this woman. All for a cat. All right, I believe what she said: it was not for the cat.

I had found that cat by a rubbish bin. Her markings looked like Newton’s rings, and I was as happy as if I had discovered gravitational waves. But I also forgot to feed her. Yifan scolded me. “You can’t even remember to eat yourself. Did you pick up a cat to starve alongside you?”

She took Banban away but gave me a key. I thought that if I could approach eternity, I would never lose them. But at the moment I completed the conversion, I suddenly realized I had already lost them. More surprising still, I felt a little attachment to the things I had thought I could easily leave behind. So I paused. Although I did not send the signal as promised, I left a turning point, hiding a polarized note in the low frequencies in F. If she used the conversion formula we had played with when we were young, she could hear a meow.

Banban was the only being who understood what I had left unfinished. I did not teach her to become light. Yet in the end she still came to my side. I knew she preferred Yifan; she slipped away to see her even more often than I did. I imagined a hundred expressions Yifan might wear after Banban disappeared. Mischievously, I even wondered whether the usually good-tempered Yifan would secretly curse me in anger: “Damn lesbian. I knew you’d steal all the cats!”

But she did not. After recognizing us, she only brushed her fingertips over the desktop and said, “Meow~”

## **III: Banban’s Traces of Light**

*On interference: they are no longer collinear, yet remain coherent.*

The first time I saw Lin An was over a messy pile of calculation papers. When she picked me up beside a roadside rubbish bin, I still had engine oil on me, and a corner of one ear was missing. She was as delighted as if she had discovered some symmetry breaking. “Your markings look like Newton’s rings!” I did not know who Newton was, but I knew she liked me.

She folded printer paper into a nest and placed me in a corner of the lab. By day there was the heat of incandescent lamps, by night the blue of fluorescent screens. I slept among equations and coffee cups. She called me Banban. But I stayed only three days. On the fourth day, a woman with a pleasant, faint tobacco scent on her fingers came, scooped me out of the paper nest, and said in an “unanswerable voice,” “Lin An, you can’t even remember to eat yourself. Did you pick up a cat to starve alongside you?” I did not actually care much whether I was hungry, but the way Lin An scratched her head in embarrassment, something she never showed before others, was truly amusing.

I was taken from the laboratory to a windowsill with just the right sunlight. There was a soft cushion, dry food, an automatic water fountain, and classical music at regular times. The person who took me away was called Shen Yifan. “Banban, welcome home,” she said. She also gave Lin An a key. Lin An always came quietly late at night, smelling all over of the laboratory. Yifan did not like talking while holding me. Lin An, however, was always noisy when she held me. She liked telling me softly about that day’s experiments, about light. She also said her soul might become part of light. I did not know what a soul was, but I knew her arms were warm.

Later I died. Shen Yifan cried. She buried me under the osmanthus tree in the yard, burned dried fish for me as offerings, and folded my little blanket neatly. Lin An did not cry, but don’t think I failed to notice her distracted experiments that day, her repeated trips out for coffee, and her habit of glancing toward the rubbish bin.

Within a month, Lin An found a kitten at the campus back gate, just as she wished. Its markings looked exactly like mine.

She laughed. “Are cat skins this easy to pull now? Banban, did you secretly bury dried fish to bribe the cat god of death?” And so I was handed to Shen Yifan again.

I came back three times in all, spending all the dried fish I had saved, and my other lives. Lin An really was a genius: even a cat’s dealings with the god of death could be guessed by her casual teasing. The one person this genius could not guess was Shen Yifan. She was always muttering and competing with me for affection. But I knew in my heart that Shen Yifan loved me for her sake.

One saw the end of the universe in light; the other held fragments of the world in dust. And I was the only bridge between them that could neither speak nor argue. Lin An took me flying; Shen Yifan fed me. Neither was perfect, but I loved them. So I kept coming back.

Until the day Lin An left.

No signal. Only a pause. This time Shen Yifan did not cry. The first thing she did on returning home was take out an old holographic imager. Holding me, she murmured, “Shouldn’t we take a hologram of Banban?”

When the holographic disc lit up, I saw myself, but not entirely myself. I saw the feeling between them that needed no language, the trust that needed no reasons. I saw the interference pattern of love.

When Lin An encountered my photonic form again, she was a little surprised. “I thought you wouldn’t bear to leave Shen Yifan.” For the first time I found the chance to tease her aloud. “Thinking about her all this time, and finally found a chance to mention that name?” Lin An became furious and refused to talk to me. So childish.

We often secretly played with Shen Yifan’s old interferometer, yet tacitly never mentioned it to one another.

I always chose afternoons with lovely sunlight to visit Shen Yifan. I jumped onto her lectern, walked in a circle, and scratched the desk a few times to sharpen my claws, just as before. Smiling, she always took out some dried fish and put them in a bowl. “Banban, welcome home.”

I had always wondered what Shen Yifan would say if she discovered Lin An.

Now I know. Cat language really is better than human language! Meow~

## **Cosmological Notebook Addendum BLN.BBN.42**

On the sixth day after the photoelectric effect failed completely, the Joint Spectral-Band Research Group issued a statement:

“We believe this is a non-hostile, system-level shutdown, possibly involving several unclassified structures of consciousness.”

This meant approximately: we know nothing, but they do not seem very interested in attacking us.

According to current information, the “Descendants of Light” are neither a species nor a civilization, but a collective of beings who have abandoned mass and their original biological classifications through multidimensional transitions. They have no clear organizational structure, no interest in diplomatic relations, and essentially no interaction with species in their original material state. Until, one day, a cat from Earth voluntarily made the transition.

The cat was reportedly called Banban (unimportant). She did something the Descendants of Light had not expected: she jumped into the spectral band and landed perfectly.
This prompted mild but widespread admiration. Some Descendants recorded her transition and published an observational log on their unstructured sharing network titled *The Banban Path: A Reproducible Route for an Unencoded, Unguided Transition*.

Soon afterward, large numbers of cats spontaneously transitioned into the realm of light, for reasons still unknown.
The prevailing view is that “after transitioning, they no longer had to let humans rub their bellies in exchange for dried fish.”

In this atmosphere, someone—more precisely, a former Earth physicist and her cat—secretly sent a modulated signal:

“We love your cat videos, but now we want cats of our own.”

Humans on Earth once mistook this signal for an official statement by the Descendants of Light, causing widespread misunderstanding in Earth’s civilization, two rounds of emergency physics reform, and a mental breakdown in one Nobel Prize judge.

But according to information archived later, this was clearly only an individual action, a harmless joke aimed at a certain individual on Earth.

After all, within the system of the Descendants of Light, no cosmic rule prevented them from doing this. And honestly, if you could pet cats, who would still be interested in tangling with boring electrons?

## **Afterword**

Some ideas are born in youth as a single sentence, such as: “They abandoned mass in exchange for eternal time.”

That was a sentence I said to a university interviewer when I was eighteen. I never forgot it, and I am glad it finally gave me the occasion to finish this lovely story.

Finally, please do not steal my cat. Meow~
